author: Riddhi Patel Santoki
title: Sector 7's Miyawaki Forest — How One Idea Turned Barren Land Green in Gandhinagar
excerpt: A few families in Sector 7A, Gandhinagar turned barren land into a thriving Miyawaki forest of over 1,000 trees — proof that a small idea, planted with intent, can grow into something a whole community benefits from.
body:
Barren land in the middle of a residential sector usually stays that way — too small for development, too neglected for anything else. In Sector 7A, Gandhinagar, one such plot sat boxed in by housing units on one side, Bharat Mata Mandir on another, and Ranchodrai Mandir at the back. Today, the same plot holds more than a thousand trees and plants, a dense Miyawaki forest that residents walk beside every day, grown from nothing more than one neighbour's idea.

It began as a hobby. My father-in-law, Dineshbhai Santoki — a landscape enthusiast living in the area— wanted to do something with the unused land near his home. He brought in his neighbour, Praveenbhai, and together planted the first batch of trees — around a hundred saplings, with no institutional backing and no formal plan beyond wanting to green a patch of dead space.

![On the left is Dineshbhai Santoki, planting a tree with a fellow resident.](/images/uploads/miyawaki-forest-elderly-residents-planting-tree-gandhinagar.webp "Dineshbhai Santoki planting a tree in Sector 7A, Gandhinagar")

**What the Miyawaki method actually does**

Father chose to plant using the Miyawaki method, a Japanese afforestation technique developed by botanist Akira Miyawaki, designed to grow dense, biodiverse forests on small plots of land in a fraction of the time natural regeneration would take. The method works by planting a wide variety of native species close together, often several saplings per square metre, which pushes the young trees to compete for sunlight and grow upward quickly rather than outward. This density also means the soil is fully shaded within a few years, which suppresses weeds, retains moisture, and builds a self-sustaining micro-ecosystem far faster than a conventional plantation.

For a plot the size of the one in Sector 7A, this made sense. A Miyawaki forest doesn't need decades to establish canopy cover, and it doesn't need heavy ongoing maintenance once it takes hold — the density of planting does most of that work on its own. What started as a hundred saplings following this method has since grown into something the neighbourhood didn't originally plan for at this scale.

**From a hundred saplings to a forest**

The planting itself became a community effort — men, women, children, and elderly residents all took turns digging and placing saplings, turning what began as one person's idea into a shared weekend activity for the whole sector.

The forest today houses more than a thousand trees and plants, grown fully organically with no chemical inputs. It has become dense enough to generate its own microclimate, noticeably cooler and more humid than the open sector around it, which has in turn drawn in a wide variety of birds and insects that would have had no reason to visit a barren plot. The forest also provides occasional fruits and vegetables to the community that planted it, turning what was once unused land into a genuine source of food alongside everything else it provides.

None of this required a large budget, a government scheme, or a developer's masterplan. It required one person willing to start, a method suited to small spaces, and neighbours willing to join in.

![Barren land in Sector 7A, Gandhinagar before the Miyawaki forest plantation began](/images/uploads/miyawaki-forest-barren-land-before-plantation-gandhinagar.webp "Barren plot in Sector 7A before Miyawaki plantation, Gandhinagar")

![Women residents planting saplings during the Miyawaki forest drive in Sector 7A, Gandhinagar](/images/uploads/miyawaki-forest-women-planting-saplings-sector-7a-gandhinagar.webp "Women planting saplings at Sector 7A Miyawaki forest, Gandhinagar")

**What this means for Gandhinagar**

Sector 7's forest is a useful reminder that meaningful green cover doesn't only come from large landscaping projects attached to big developments. The Miyawaki method exists precisely for situations like this — small, awkward plots that nobody has a plan for, turned into dense, self-sustaining forests within a few years rather than decades. A barren plot surrounded by homes and temples, given the right method and a handful of committed hands, can become a working ecosystem that cools the immediate area, provides occasional fruits and vegetables to the people around it, and gives space back to birds and insects that have nowhere else to go in a dense residential sector. It started with one idea and a hundred saplings. It's now a forest, and still growing — one small step towards making the green city of Gandhinagar even greener.
